title: Poor Proxies #2: The Engagement Myth
author: Jamie Clark
summary: In the second Poor Proxies instalment, Clark challenges the idea that motivated, interested students must be learning. Drawing on Rob Coe's framework and Willingham's claim that students remember what they think about, he argues that enjoyment can be cognitively empty and that fun activities can pull attention away from the core content. He cites Kirschner, Sweller and Clark on novices needing explicit guidance rather than discovery. The central claim is that engagement is a starting point whose value depends on whether it points at the right target. His prescription is to design tasks in which the interesting thing and the hard thinking are the same thing, and to ask what students are thinking about rather than whether they are engaged.
points: Engagement is not learning: a lesson can be enjoyable and cognitively empty at the same time.
Because students remember what they think about, activities that draw attention to the activity rather than the content make engagement decorative.
Enjoyment, activity, motivation and interest are each mistaken for understanding, thinking, effort and learning respectively.
Novices benefit from explicit guidance, and unguided engagement may not produce the schema-building that yields understanding.
The better question is what students are thinking about, with tasks that make interest and cognitive effort point the same way.
quotes: The Engagement Myth is the belief that because students are interested, motivated, and enjoying a lesson, learning must be happening. It's one of the most widely held assumptions in teaching — and one of the most misleading.
Coe identified student engagement as a poor proxy because, while it often accompanies learning, it doesn't guarantee it. A lesson can be thoroughly enjoyable and cognitively empty at the same time.

The issue isn't engagement itself — it's when we use it as our primary signal that learning is occurring. As cognitive scientist Daniel Willingham reminds us, the brain isn't naturally drawn to thinking hard. It's drawn to interest — and the two don't always overlap.

A student absorbed in a group work, a creative task, or an insightful video might be highly engaged — but if that activity isn't directing their attention toward the core content they need to learn, the engagement is essentially decorative.

The Engagement Myth matters because it quietly shapes lesson design in ways that prioritise enjoyment over thinking. When we believe engagement signals learning, we design for engagement — and the cognitive work becomes optional.
This means that highly engaging lessons — ones built around exciting stimuli, entertainment, or open-ended exploration — can actually reduce the amount of hard thinking students do, not increase it.
This is why the question to ask isn't "Are students engaged?" — it's "What are students thinking about?" Engagement is welcome. But it needs to be pointed at the right target.
